analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug makers from paying generic and biosimilar makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a bipartisan pair of senators with 7 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company sues a generic maker over a patent, the two sometimes settle with the brand company paying the generic company to stay off the market — a "reverse payment" that keeps cheaper copies off pharmacy shelves. This bill would let the Federal Trade Commission treat such pay-for-delay deals as anticompetitive by default, with penalties up to triple the value exchanged, and would require drug companies to certify under oath that they have disclosed every side agreement and oral promise to the FTC and the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescription drugs — consumers, employers, and taxpayers, who fund over 40% of retail prescription drug spending. Generic drugs cost 80–85% less than brand-name versions, so faster generic and biosimilar entry means lower prices and more access.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who pay for drugs

how_it_helps.text: Creates a presumption that a patent settlement in which the generic or biosimilar filer receives something of value and agrees to delay its product is anticompetitive, shifting the burden to the drug companies to prove otherwise.

Authorizes the FTC to bring enforcement proceedings against pay-for-delay settlements and impose civil penalties up to three times the value received, plus forfeiture of the generic filer's 180-day marketing exclusivity as a deterrent.

Requires company officials to certify that filings with the FTC and Justice Department include the complete agreement plus any related side agreements, written descriptions of oral promises, and contingent deals.

The bill's findings note generics sell at discounts averaging 80–85% off brand prices and account for 88% of prescriptions but only 28% of drug spending, so earlier generic entry directly cuts what patients and payers spend.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies would lose the ability to pay off generic challengers and extend monopoly profits past patent expiration, and generic makers taking delay payments could forfeit their first-filer exclusivity and face penalties.

drawbacks.text: A good-faith objection: not every settlement with a payment is anticompetitive — some reflect genuine uncertainty about whether a patent would hold, and litigation is expensive; the bill lets parties escape the presumption only by proving procompetitive benefits by clear and convincing evidence, a heavy bar.

Stronger antitrust pressure on settlements could make brand and generic companies more hesitant to settle patent disputes at all, producing longer and costlier litigation whose costs may show up in drug prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific practice the record describes as splitting monopoly profits between brand and generic makers at consumers' expense, and it carves out ordinary settlements (early entry rights, litigation-cost payments up to $7.5 million, covenants not to sue). The main cost is borne by the drug companies whose pay-for-delay arrangements would be curtailed; the design is targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar, joined by Senator Grassley, introduced the bill on January 9, 2019, making it a bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The bill attracted 7 cosponsors — 4 Republicans and 3 Democrats — but the Judiciary Committee never took it up before the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies keep the ability to settle patent suits by paying generic rivals to delay market entry, preserving extended monopoly pricing that consumers and health payers continue to fund.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit brand companies from compensating generic and biosimilar makers to delay market entry.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined Klobuchar in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 7 senators (4 Republicans, 3 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding bipartisan support.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Lindsey Graham (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without any vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose pay-for-delay settlements the bill targets
against.what_they_did: The bill was written to prohibit their reverse-payment settlements; similar bills died without floor votes in this era, with the industry a prominent opponent of such measures.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic lead sponsor with a Republican co-lead and 4 of 7 cosponsors Republican — so the bill died in committee without a party-line fight ever being tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to pay generic challengers to stay off the market, ending a tool that extends monopoly pricing after patent expiry. Consumers and payers bear that cost today in higher drug prices.

Faster market entry would benefit honest generic competitors, but companies taking delay payments would face penalties up to triple the value received and forfeiture of their 180-day first-filer exclusivity. The bill preserves legitimate settlements for early entry, litigation costs, and covenants not to sue.
